title: If I perish (Esther 4:16, 7)
hookLine: Esther says "if I perish, I perish", and names the enemy at her banquet
last: FOR SUCH A TIME AS THIS.

cards: Esther's reply is short, and it's an order. Go, gather all the Jews in Shushan, and fast for me. Don't eat or drink for three days, night or day.
My maids and I will fast too. Then I'll go in to the king, which is not according to the law. And she ends with a line that sounds almost like a shrug: "and if I perish, I perish."
Something has flipped. Back in chapter two, Mordecai gave the orders and Esther kept quiet. Now the text says Mordecai went his way and "did according to all that Esther had commanded him."

teach.b: If I perish, I perish. It isn't despair. It's a person counting the cost before she moves, and then moving.
Esther doesn't pretend the danger is small. She names it, prepares, and goes. On the third day she puts on her royal clothes and stands in the inner court.
The king sees her and holds out the golden scepter. She lives. He offers her anything, up to half the kingdom.
And here's the surprise: she doesn't blurt out her request. She invites the king and Haman to a banquet. At the banquet, she invites them to another.
Some readers call it stalling; others, strategy: she's choosing the room, the hour, and the moment the king is ready to listen.
At the second banquet, in chapter seven, she finally speaks, and ties her own life to her people's: "let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request."
The secret she kept since chapter two is out loud now.
"For we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish."
Perish again, the same word she risked for herself.
The king asks who would dare.
And she names him to his face: "The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman." Before the chapter ends, Haman is hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai.
The story still has chapters to run, but the turn happens here, at a dinner table, when one person says the name.

how: The day before Purim is kept by tradition as the Fast of Esther, Ta'anit Esther, which recalls the fast she asked of the Jews of Shushan before she went in to the king.

practice: Bring to mind one person who isn't in the room when things about them get decided: a coworker, a neighbor, a child, someone easy to forget. Find the sentence you'd say for them if you were asked, plain, kind and true.
If you pray, hold that person before God in words from your tradition.

wordCard.voice: Haman, the enemy Esther finally names to the king's face, at the banquet she arranged after risking her life to be heard. Today's word.
